name: Vertebral column
description: The 24 presacral vertebrae (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar) and the sacrum.

source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved). Shapes simplified for the web only.
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, meshes simplified with quadric decimation for web delivery, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred, one node per structure. Structures marked "merged" are the union of several BodyParts3D meshes (e.g. the parts of one muscle); structures with a "component" take one connected part of a BodyParts3D mesh, chosen by position.

groups.label: Vertebral column
groups.tip: Breakfast at seven, lunch at twelve, dinner at five: seven neck, twelve chest and five lower back vertebrae. Then come the fused sacrum and coccyx.

groups.label: Cervical vertebrae
groups.tip: Only neck vertebrae have a small hole on each side for an artery. C one lets you nod yes, and C two lets you shake your head no.

groups.label: Thoracic vertebrae
groups.tip: Only chest vertebrae have joints for the ribs. From the side they look like a giraffe's head, with a long spine pointing down.

groups.label: Lumbar vertebrae
groups.tip: Lower back vertebrae have the biggest, kidney-shaped bodies and short, square spines. They grow larger as you go down, because they carry more weight.

groups.label: Sacrum
groups.tip: Five sacral vertebrae fuse into one triangle, the sacrum. It locks into your pelvis at the two sacroiliac joints.

content.origin: Named after Atlas, the giant of Greek myth who held up the sky. This bone holds up your head.
content.location: The very top of your spine, tucked right under the base of your skull. The axis, C2, sits just below it.
content.description: A simple ring of bone, with no solid body and no spine sticking out at the back. Wide side wings each have a small hole in them.
content.function: It carries your skull and lets you nod yes. When you shake your head no, this ring swivels around a peg on the bone below.
content.mnemonic: Atlas holds up the world, your head, and says yes. The axis below it says no.
content.clinical: A heavy blow straight down on the top of the head, like diving into shallow water, can burst this ring. This is called a Jefferson fracture.
content.hint: The very first bone of the spine, a ring with no body that the skull rests on.

questions.text: Which vertebra has no body and no spinous process?
questions.explanation: The atlas, C1, is just a ring of bone with a front arch, a back arch and two side masses. It has no body at all.

questions.text: The joints between the atlas and the skull mainly let your head do what?
questions.explanation: The skull rocks forward and back on the atlas, so you can nod yes.

content.origin: From the Latin word for an axle or pivot. Your head and the atlas turn around it like a wheel on an axle.
content.location: The second bone of your neck, just below the atlas and above C3.
content.description: You can spot it by the dens, a tooth-shaped peg that points up into the ring above. Its big, forked spine can be felt high at the back of your neck.
content.function: It is the pivot for turning your head. The atlas and skull spin around its peg when you shake your head no, giving about half of your neck's turning.
content.mnemonic: The Axis is the Axle. Your head turns around its tooth, the dens.
content.clinical: Older people can break the peg in a fall. A hangman's fracture breaks both sides of the arch of C2 when the head is forced far back.
content.hint: Look just under the top ring for a bone with a tooth-shaped peg poking upward.

questions.text: What is the tooth-like peg on the axis called?
questions.explanation: The dens, also called the odontoid process, means tooth-like. It points up from the axis into the ring of the atlas.

questions.text: Shaking your head to say no mainly happens at which joint?
questions.explanation: At the atlanto-axial joint, the atlas and skull spin around the peg of the axis.

content.origin: From the Latin word cervix, meaning neck. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn, because the spine lets you twist and bend.
content.location: The third bone of your neck, just below the axis. It sits at about the level of the hyoid, the small U-shaped bone above your voice box.
content.description: The first typical neck vertebra, small and light. It has an oval body, a short spine split into two tips, and a small hole in each side wing.
content.function: It helps hold up your head and lets your neck move. The holes in its side wings carry the arteries that climb up to your brain.
content.mnemonic: C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive. The nerve to your breathing muscle starts at this level.
content.clinical: A spinal cord injury around C3 to C5 can cut the nerve supply to the diaphragm. These people may need a machine to help them breathe.
content.hint: Count down the neck to the first ordinary bone, right under the one with the tooth-shaped peg.

questions.text: Why is a spinal cord injury around C3 to C5 so dangerous?
options: It can affect the nerve to the diaphragm and breathing
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve to the diaphragm comes from C3, C4 and C5. Damage here can stop you breathing on your own.

content.origin: From the Latin word cervix, meaning neck. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn, because the spine lets you twist and bend.
content.location: The fourth bone of your neck, in the middle between C3 and C5. It sits about level with the top of your voice box.
content.description: A small neck vertebra with an oval body, a triangle-shaped hole for the cord and a short spine split into two tips. Each side wing has its own little hole.
content.function: It helps hold up your head and lets you bend, tilt and turn your neck. The holes in its side wings carry the vertebral artery and vein.
content.mnemonic: Think of C4 as the fork for the carotid. The big neck artery usually splits into two at about C3 to C4.
content.clinical: The carotid artery usually splits near C3 to C4, level with the top of the voice box. This fork is a common place for fatty build-up that narrows the artery.
content.hint: Find the middle one of the seven neck bones, about level with the top of the voice box.

questions.text: The common carotid artery usually splits in two at about which level?
questions.explanation: The carotid artery usually forks at about C3 to C4, level with the top of the voice box.

content.origin: From the Latin word cervix, meaning neck. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn, because the spine lets you twist and bend.
content.location: The fifth bone of your neck, between C4 and C6, in the lower half of the neck.
content.description: A small neck vertebra with an oval body, a triangle-shaped hole for the cord and a short spine split into two tips. Each side wing has its own little hole.
content.function: It helps hold up your head and lets your neck move. The lower neck around C5 and C6 does a lot of the bending forward and back.
content.mnemonic: C5 to C6 is the busiest junction of the neck, so it wears out first.
content.clinical: The disc between C5 and C6 is one of the most common to wear out or bulge. It can press on a nerve and send pain down the arm.
content.hint: In the lower half of the neck, one level above the bone level with the cricoid cartilage.

questions.text: Wear and tear of the neck discs is most common at which level?
questions.explanation: The lower neck, especially C5 to C6, moves the most, so its discs wear out most often.

content.origin: From the Latin word cervix, meaning neck. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn, because the spine lets you twist and bend.
content.location: The sixth bone of your neck, level with the cricoid cartilage. Here the voice box becomes the windpipe and the throat becomes the food pipe.
content.description: A small neck vertebra with an oval body, a triangle-shaped hole for the cord and a short spine split into two tips. Each side wing has its own little hole.
content.function: It helps hold up your head and lets your neck move. The vertebral artery usually enters the hole in its side wing on the way up to the brain.
content.mnemonic: Six for switch. At C6 the voice box switches to the windpipe and the throat switches to the food pipe.
content.clinical: A large bump on the front of its side wing, the carotid tubercle, lets you press the carotid artery against it. It also guides some nerve blocks in the neck.
content.hint: Look low in the neck, level with the ring of cartilage where the voice box meets the windpipe.

questions.text: At the level of C6, the throat, or pharynx, becomes which tube?
questions.explanation: At C6 the throat carries on as the oesophagus, your food pipe, and the voice box carries on as the windpipe.

questions.text: The vertebral artery usually enters the side holes of the neck bones at which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The vertebral artery usually enters the hole in C6, then climbs up through the holes above it.

content.origin: Its Latin name, vertebra prominens, means the prominent vertebra. Its spine sticks out at the base of your neck.
content.location: The lowest bone of your neck, sitting on top of T1, the first chest vertebra.
content.description: It has a long, single spine that you can easily feel at the base of your neck. Its side holes are small and usually carry only small veins, not the vertebral artery.
content.function: It links the bendy neck to the stiffer chest spine. The strong ligament at the back of the neck and several back muscles hold on to it.
content.mnemonic: C7 is the bump at the base of your neck. Bend your head forward and feel for it.
content.clinical: Doctors use its bump as a starting point to count down the spine. Now and then an extra rib grows from C7 and squeezes the nerves or vessels to the arm.
content.hint: Go to the base of the neck and find the bone with the longest, easiest bump to feel.

questions.text: Why is C7 called the vertebra prominens?
options: Its long spine is easy to feel at the base of the neck
It has the largest body in the spine
questions.explanation: C7 has a long spine without a split tip. It sticks out as the bump at the base of your neck.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The first chest vertebra, just below C7 at the base of your neck.
content.description: A mix of neck and chest shapes. Its body looks like a neck vertebra, with a full joint surface for the first rib and a half surface below for the second.
content.function: It holds the first pair of ribs and forms the back of the top of the chest. The windpipe, food pipe and big blood vessels pass through this opening.
content.mnemonic: T1 wears the first rib like a collar, with one full facet for rib one.
content.clinical: The T1 nerve helps supply the hand. A lung tumour at the very top of the chest can press on it and make the hand weak.
content.hint: Look just below the big bump at the base of the neck, where the first pair of ribs join.

questions.text: The first rib joins a full joint surface on which vertebra?
questions.explanation: T1 has a full facet, a small joint surface, for the head of the first rib.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The second chest vertebra, in your upper back. The notch at the top of your breastbone sits about level with the disc between T2 and T3.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the second and third ribs and helps hold up the top of the rib cage.
content.mnemonic: T2 tops the sternum. The notch at the top of your breastbone lines up with T2 to T3.
content.clinical: These upper chest bones are handy landmarks on chest X-rays. Feel the dip at the top of your breastbone, and you are level with the T2 to T3 disc.
content.hint: Count two bones into the chest spine, level with the dip at the top of the breastbone.

questions.text: The notch at the top of the breastbone is usually level with which part of the spine?
questions.explanation: The jugular notch, the dip at the top of your breastbone, lines up with the disc between T2 and T3.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The third chest vertebra, in your upper back. Its spine lines up with the inner end of the bony ridge on each shoulder blade.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the third and fourth ribs. Back muscles like the trapezius and rhomboids hold on to it to steady your shoulder blades.
content.mnemonic: Three for the scapular spine. Draw a line between the inner ends of the shoulder blade ridges and you hit T3.
content.clinical: With the arms relaxed by the sides, the inner end of each shoulder blade ridge is level with T3. This helps you count the chest vertebrae.
content.hint: In the upper back, look level with the inner ends of the ridges on the shoulder blades.

questions.text: With the arms relaxed, the inner end of the shoulder blade ridge is level with which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The inner end of the spine of the scapula lines up with the T3 spinous process.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The fourth chest vertebra. The disc below it lines up with the sternal angle, the small ridge you can feel near the top of your breastbone.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the fourth and fifth ribs. At the T4 to T5 level, the windpipe splits in two and the arch of the aorta begins and ends.
content.mnemonic: T4 is the fork. The windpipe forks near T4 to T5, level with the sternal angle.
content.clinical: The sternal angle lines up with the T4 to T5 disc. It helps you find the second rib and marks where the windpipe splits into the two lungs.
content.hint: Find the chest bone whose disc below lines up with the small ridge near the top of the breastbone.

questions.text: The sternal angle lies level with which disc?
questions.explanation: The sternal angle is level with the T4 to T5 disc. The windpipe splits and the aortic arch sits at this level.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The fifth chest vertebra, in the middle of your upper back. It sits right behind your heart and food pipe.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the fifth and sixth ribs. Together with the ribs and breastbone it forms a cage that guards your heart and lungs.
content.mnemonic: From the side, a chest vertebra looks like a giraffe's head, with the long spine as the neck pointing down.
content.clinical: Your chest spine has a natural backward curve, called kyphosis. Poor posture, a growth problem in teenagers or fragile bones in older age can make it too curved.
content.hint: Look behind the heart, one bone below the level of the ridge near the top of the breastbone.

questions.text: The normal backward curve of the chest spine is called what?
questions.explanation: Kyphosis is the normal gentle hump of the chest spine, curving backward.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The sixth chest vertebra, in the middle of your back between T5 and T7.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the sixth and seventh ribs. It helps support the chest wall and lets your trunk twist a little.
content.mnemonic: The T6 rule. A cord injury at six or higher can trigger autonomic dysreflexia.
content.clinical: After a spinal cord injury at or above about T6, something small like a full bladder can make blood pressure shoot up. This is called autonomic dysreflexia.
content.hint: In the middle of the back, look one bone above the level of the shoulder blade tips.

questions.text: A cord injury at or above about which level puts people at risk of autonomic dysreflexia?
questions.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia, a sudden dangerous rise in blood pressure, mainly happens with cord injuries at or above about T6.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The seventh chest vertebra, in your mid back. With your arms by your sides, its spine lines up with the lower tips of your shoulder blades.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the seventh and eighth ribs. The seventh rib is the last true rib, the lowest one with its own cartilage straight to the breastbone.
content.mnemonic: T7 is the tip of the scapula. The lower tip of each shoulder blade points to T7.
content.clinical: The lower tip of the shoulder blade is a handy guide to T7. Doctors use it to count vertebrae and when listening to the lungs from behind.
content.hint: Look in the mid back, level with the lower tips of the shoulder blades.

questions.text: The lower tip of the shoulder blade is usually level with which vertebra?
questions.explanation: With your arms by your sides, the lower tip of the shoulder blade lines up with the spine of T7.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The eighth chest vertebra, between T7 and T9, in the lower half of your chest spine.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the eighth and ninth ribs. The inferior vena cava, the big vein from your lower body, passes through the diaphragm at about this level.
content.mnemonic: I 8 10 Eggs At 12. The vena cava passes at T8, the oesophagus at T10 and the aorta at T12.
content.clinical: The big vein from the lower body passes through an opening in the diaphragm's central tendon at about T8. This opening is called the caval opening.
content.hint: Look low in the chest spine, where the big vein from the lower body pierces the diaphragm.

questions.text: The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at about which level?
questions.explanation: The caval opening sits at about T8. Remember I 8 10 Eggs At 12.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The ninth chest vertebra, between T8 and T10. The joint at the lower end of your breastbone lines up with it.
content.description: A typical chest vertebra with a heart-shaped body and small joint surfaces for the ribs. Its long spine slopes down like a roof tile.
content.function: It joins the ninth and tenth ribs. It helps support the lower chest wall, where the diaphragm holds on.
content.mnemonic: Nine at the xiphoid. The bottom of your breastbone lines up with T9.
content.clinical: In older people with fragile bones, the lower chest vertebrae can collapse at the front into a wedge. This causes back pain and loss of height.
content.hint: Look low in the chest spine, level with the bottom tip of the breastbone.

questions.text: Which fracture often affects chest vertebrae in older people with fragile bones?
questions.explanation: In osteoporosis the weakened vertebral body squashes down at the front, making a wedge shape.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The tenth chest vertebra, between T9 and T11, low in your chest spine.
content.description: Much like a typical chest vertebra, but its body often has one full joint surface for the tenth rib instead of two halves. Its long spine slopes down.
content.function: It joins the tenth rib. Your food pipe passes through the diaphragm at about this level.
content.mnemonic: I 8 10 Eggs At 12. Oesophagus has ten letters, and it passes through at T10.
content.clinical: The food pipe passes through a gap in the diaphragm at about T10. In a hiatus hernia, part of the stomach slides up through this gap into the chest.
content.hint: Look low in the chest spine, where the food pipe passes through the diaphragm.

questions.text: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm at about which level?
questions.explanation: The food pipe goes through the oesophageal hiatus at about T10. Oesophagus even has ten letters.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The second last chest vertebra, between T10 and T12, near the bottom of your chest spine.
content.description: An unusual chest vertebra. Its body has one full joint surface for the eleventh rib, and its side wings have none. Its bigger body starts to look like a lower back bone.
content.function: It holds the head of the eleventh rib, a floating rib that never reaches the breastbone.
content.mnemonic: Eleven and twelve float free. T11 and T12 carry the floating ribs.
content.clinical: The lower chest spine, near where it meets the lower back, is a common place to break the spine in a fall or a car crash.
content.hint: The second-last chest vertebra, carrying a floating rib with no facet on its side wing.

questions.text: Why do the side wings of T11 have no rib facets?
options: The eleventh rib does not attach to them
They are fused to the sacrum
The facets are on the spinous process instead
questions.explanation: The eleventh rib joins only the body of T11. It never touches the side wings, so they need no joint surface.

content.origin: Thoracic comes from the Greek word for a breastplate, or chest. Vertebra comes from a Latin word meaning to turn.
content.location: The last chest vertebra, sitting on top of L1, where your chest spine turns into your lower back.
content.description: A halfway bone. Its upper joints face like a chest vertebra and its lower joints like a lower back one. It has one full facet for the twelfth rib and a big body.
content.function: It holds the twelfth rib and links the stiff, rib-bearing chest spine to the bendy lower back. The aorta passes behind the diaphragm at this level.
content.mnemonic: I 8 10 Eggs At 12. The Aorta passes through at T12.
content.clinical: The T12 to L1 junction is one of the most common places to break the spine. Stress builds up where the stiff chest spine meets the bendy lower back.
content.hint: Find the last bone that carries a rib, where the chest spine turns into the lower back.

questions.text: Why does the spine often break around T12 to L1?
options: The stiff chest spine meets the bendy lower back
questions.explanation: Stress piles up where the stiff chest spine joins the bendy lower back, like a bend in a garden hose.

questions.text: The aorta passes the diaphragm at about which level?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus sits at about T12. Remember I 8 10 Eggs At 12.

content.origin: Lumbar comes from the Latin word for the loin, your lower back. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn.
content.location: The first bone of your lower back, just below T12. The plane doctors use to find the exit of the stomach runs at about this level.
content.description: A big, chunky lower back vertebra with a kidney-shaped body and a short, square spine like a hatchet. It has no rib facets and no holes in its side wings.
content.function: It carries the weight of your upper body. In adults, the lower tip of the spinal cord usually ends at about L1 to L2.
content.mnemonic: The cord stops at L1 to 2. Below it hangs the cauda equina, a horse's tail of nerve roots.
content.clinical: Because the cord ends near L1 to L2 in adults, a spinal tap needle goes in lower down, at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5, well clear of the cord.
content.hint: Go one bone below the last rib-bearing bone, to the top of the lower back.

questions.text: In adults, the spinal cord usually ends at about which level?
questions.explanation: The cord tapers to an end at about L1 to L2 in adults. Below that is only a bundle of nerve roots.

content.origin: Lumbar comes from the Latin word for the loin, your lower back. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn.
content.location: The second bone of your lower back, between L1 and L3.
content.description: A big, chunky lower back vertebra with a kidney-shaped body and a short, square spine like a hatchet. It has no rib facets and no holes in its side wings.
content.function: It carries your upper body's weight and lets your lower back bend and tilt. The legs of the diaphragm and the big psoas muscle hold on to these upper lumbar bones.
content.mnemonic: The lower you go, the bigger they grow. Lumbar bodies are big because they carry the load.
content.clinical: Below about L2, the canal holds nerve roots, not cord. A large slipped disc here can squash them, called cauda equina syndrome, and it needs urgent surgery.
content.hint: Count two bones down into the lower back, just below where the cord usually ends.

questions.text: The bundle of nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord is called what?
questions.explanation: Cauda equina means horse's tail. It is the bundle of lower nerve roots hanging below the end of the cord.

content.origin: Lumbar comes from the Latin word for the loin, your lower back. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn.
content.location: The third bone of your lower back, right in the middle of the five, near the level of your belly button.
content.description: A big, chunky lower back vertebra with a kidney-shaped body and a short, square spine like a hatchet. It has no rib facets and no holes in its side wings.
content.function: It carries weight at the middle of the lower back curve. It usually has the longest side wings of the lumbar bones, giving back muscles good leverage.
content.mnemonic: L3 sits in the middle of the lordosis, the inward curve of your lower back.
content.clinical: A spinal tap is usually done between L3 and L4, or L4 and L5. This is below the end of the cord, so fluid can be taken safely.
content.hint: Pick the middle one of the five lower back bones, the one with the longest side wings.

questions.text: A spinal tap, or lumbar puncture, is usually done at which level?
options: L3 to L4 or L4 to L5
questions.explanation: These gaps are below the end of the spinal cord, so the needle is unlikely to hurt it.

questions.text: The normal inward curve of the lower back is called what?
questions.explanation: Lordosis is the normal inward curve of the lower back, the hollow just above your bottom.

content.origin: Lumbar comes from the Latin word for the loin, your lower back. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn.
content.location: The fourth bone of your lower back. A line joining the tops of your hip bones crosses about the L4 spine, or the gap just below it.
content.description: A big, chunky lower back vertebra with a kidney-shaped body and a short, square spine like a hatchet. It has no rib facets and no holes in its side wings.
content.function: It carries body weight and lets your lower back move. The aorta splits into the two arteries for the legs just in front of it.
content.mnemonic: Hands on hips find L4. Put your thumbs on the tops of your hip bones and they point to L4.
content.clinical: The discs below L4 and below L5 slip out more than any others. A slipped disc can press on a nerve root and send sciatica pain down the leg.
content.hint: Look in the lower back, level with the tops of the hip bones.

questions.text: A line joining the tops of the hip bones helps you find which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The line across the top of the iliac crests passes about the L4 spine or the gap just below it.

questions.text: The abdominal aorta splits into the two common iliac arteries at about which level?
questions.explanation: The aorta forks in two just in front of the body of L4.

content.origin: Lumbar comes from the Latin word for the loin, your lower back. Vertebra comes from a word meaning to turn.
content.location: The last bone of your lower back, sitting right on top of the sacrum.
content.description: The largest vertebra of all. Its body is taller at the front than the back, like a wedge, which sets the angle where the lower back meets the sacrum.
content.function: It passes the weight of your upper body down to the sacrum and pelvis. Strong ligaments tie its thick side wings to the hip bones.
content.mnemonic: L5 is the largest and the last. The biggest body carries the most weight.
content.clinical: A stress crack in its arch, and the bone slipping forward, are most common at L5. Young athletes who arch their backs a lot, like gymnasts and fast bowlers, are at risk.
content.hint: Find the biggest and lowest bone of the lower back, resting on the fused wedge below.

questions.text: A vertebra slipping forward on the one below most often involves which bone?
questions.explanation: This slip, called spondylolisthesis, is most common at L5, where the shearing force on the lower back is greatest.

questions.text: Which is the largest vertebra in the spine?
questions.explanation: L5 has the biggest body, because it carries the most weight before it reaches the sacrum.

content.origin: From the Latin os sacrum, the sacred bone, copied from an older Greek name. Nobody knows for sure why it was called sacred.
content.location: At the base of your spine, below L5, wedged between your two hip bones at the back of the pelvis. The tailbone hangs from its lower tip.
content.description: A big triangle made of five vertebrae fused together. It has four pairs of holes for nerves and an ear-shaped joint surface on each side.
content.function: It passes the weight of your upper body into the pelvis through the sacroiliac joints. It also forms the back wall of the pelvis and lets the sacral nerves out.
content.mnemonic: Breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5, and 5 fused for dessert. That is 7 neck, 12 chest, 5 lower back and 5 sacral bones.
content.clinical: The sacroiliac joints are a common source of low back and buttock pain. A gap at the bottom of the sacrum lets doctors inject numbing medicine, often in children.
content.hint: Look at the back of the pelvis for a big triangle of fused bones between the two hip bones.

questions.text: How many vertebrae fuse together to make the sacrum?
questions.explanation: The sacrum is five sacral vertebrae, S1 to S5, fused into one strong triangle.

questions.text: The sacrum joins the hip bones at which joints?
questions.explanation: The ear-shaped surfaces on the sides of the sacrum meet the hip bones at the sacroiliac joints.
